vignette:
Ravi had always thought of himself as someone who could handle things. At twenty-six, he was an editor at a mid-sized publishing house in Chicago, a job that required patience, precision, and a quiet confidence in his own judgment. He had been married for two years to Priya, a nurse who worked long shifts but always came home with a warm laugh and a steady presence. Their life was small but full-dinner with friends on weekends, plans for a child in the next year or two, a shared sense that things were moving in the right direction. That was before the night in late October when he took the wrong train home.

It had been raining, and the platform at the Howard Street station was nearly empty. Ravi had been waiting for the Purple Line when two officers approached him. He did not remember what they said first. He remembered the cold. The air was sharp with the onset of winter, and the rain had soaked through his jacket, plastering his shirt to his chest. One of the officers grabbed his arm, and the other pushed him against the concrete wall. The cold of the wall went through his clothes and into his back, a specific, penetrating cold that he would later feel again in his own living room, in his own bed, at odd moments when the thermostat dipped below a certain point. He remembered the smell of the officer's cologne-something cheap and sharp, like artificial pine-mixed with the wet metal of the train tracks and the damp wool of his own coat. He remembered being on the ground, his cheek pressed against the cold concrete, his arm twisted behind him, and the weight of a knee in the small of his back. He had not resisted. He had not said a word. But they had held him there for what felt like an hour, though it was probably ten minutes, while they ran his ID. They let him go with a warning not to loiter. He had not been charged with anything. He had not done anything.

The first weeks after, Ravi told himself it was over. He was fine. But the memories did not come as stories; they came as smells. He would be walking through the grocery store and suddenly catch a whiff of pine-scented cleaner, and his chest would tighten, and his mouth would go dry. He would be sitting at his desk editing a manuscript, and the air from the vent would blow across his neck, and he would feel the cold concrete against his cheek again, his body going rigid in his chair, his arm instinctively pulling behind his back. He began to avoid the break room because a female colleague from marketing liked to sit in there alone, and being in the room with her, just the two of them, made his heart race for no reason he could name. He started taking the stairs instead of the elevator because the enclosed space felt like a trap. He stopped going to the office gym because the locker room smelled like damp towels and industrial cleaner, and that combination sent him straight back to the platform.

The worst part, though, was what happened inside his own head. Ravi had always believed that if you worked hard and did the right things, life would make sense. But now nothing made sense. He had done nothing wrong, and still they had put him on the ground. He had frozen, had not fought back, had not even asked why. He replayed that moment of paralysis again and again, and each time he came to the same conclusion: he had been a coward. A real man, a strong person, would have stood up for himself. He had not. He was a lousy coper. He had fallen apart over a ten-minute misunderstanding, and now he could not even sit in a room with a woman alone without his hands shaking. What kind of husband was he? What kind of father would he ever be?

The meaning drained out of everything. His work, which he had once loved, felt hollow. He would stare at a page of text and see only words, nothing that mattered. Priya would talk about their plans, and he would nod, but inside he felt nothing. He was certain that nothing good could happen to him anymore. The world had shown him what it really was, and he had seen that he was not equipped for it. He had come to believe that he was broken in some fundamental way, that the event had not just scared him but had revealed a truth about himself that he had been hiding from.

The grief caught him off guard. It was not fear that flooded him when he remembered that night-it was a deep, overwhelming grief, as though he had lost someone. And in a way, he had. He had lost the person he thought he was. He had lost the belief that the world was fair, that he was safe, that his life had a direction. He would be standing in the shower, and the water would hit his back at a certain angle, and suddenly he would be back on that cold ground, and the grief would rise in his chest like a wave, and he would have to brace himself against the tile to keep from sinking to his knees.

Priya noticed. Of course she noticed. He was distant. He flinched when she touched him unexpectedly. He had stopped going out with friends. He spent his evenings on the couch, staring at the television without seeing it. She asked him what was wrong, and he said he was tired. She asked him again, and he said work was stressful. She asked him a third time, and he told her about the train platform. He told her the facts, but he could not tell her what it felt like, because he did not have the words. She held him and said it was not his fault. He wanted to believe her, but he knew what he knew. He had not fought. He had not spoken. He had lain there on the cold ground and taken it.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a moment at work two weeks ago. He was in a meeting with his boss, a woman named Sarah, and the door clicked shut behind her. The room was cold-the air conditioning was always too strong in that conference room-and he felt the cold on his arms, on his neck, and suddenly he could not breathe. He felt his body go still, felt his arm begin to drift behind his back, felt himself starting to float away from the room, as though he were watching himself from above. Sarah asked him a question, and he could not answer. He sat there, frozen, until she opened the door and the air changed. He excused himself and went to the bathroom and stood over the sink, gripping the porcelain, trying to find his way back into his own body. That night, he told Priya he needed help.

He is here now, sitting in a chair that is too soft, in a room that is too warm, trying to find the words. He does not know if talking will help. He is afraid that it will only confirm what he already suspects-that he is too weak to fix this, that the grief will never lift, that the cold will follow him forever. But he is also afraid of what will happen if he does not try. He is afraid of losing Priya. He is afraid of losing himself entirely. And so he sits, and he waits, and he begins.
